cim: High Growth Artificial Intelligence Stocks: Morningstar Picks
cim_eredeti: High Growth Artificial Intelligence Stocks: Morningstar Picks
szoveg_eredeti:
High growth artificial intelligence stocks Nvidia, Microsoft and Amazon were trading below Morningstar’s fair value estimates in a roundup dated Oct. 19, 2026. Morningstar described the three companies as undervalued by 31%, 12% and 17%, respectively, and assigned the listed stocks 4- or 5-star ratings.

The figures are Morningstar’s estimates, not forecasts of how much the shares will rise. The roundup’s publication date is Oct. 14, while its stock data is dated Oct. 19, so the valuations should be read as estimates for that date rather than current prices.

Morningstar’s stock roundup connects the three companies to different parts of the AI economy: Nvidia supplies computing hardware and software, Microsoft offers cloud services and business software, and Amazon operates a large cloud business alongside its retail operations.

Morningstar said its 4- and 5-star-rated picks were undervalued as of Oct. 19. The source does not frame that rating as a growth forecast; its fair value comparisons instead describe the gap between the firm’s estimate and the shares’ market valuation on the stated date.

The selection also reflects a broader distinction between a company’s connection to AI and the basis for its valuation. Nvidia’s profile centers on chips, software and networking used in AI infrastructure. Microsoft’s case combines cloud delivery and AI with established software products and customer relationships. Amazon is included as a major cloud provider, but the available company discussion emphasizes its retail and cloud-market position rather than detailing specific AI offerings.

The roundup places those company assessments against a sharp change in the sector’s mood. It describes October as resembling March, when semiconductor shares sold off and investors worried about debt-funded investment in AI infrastructure. That pressure arrived ahead of earnings season even as the Morningstar Global Next Generation Artificial Intelligence Index had risen more than 29% year to date and about 45% during the spring. The index’s performance describes the basket, not the return of each stock in this article.

Nvidia develops graphics processing units, or GPUs, and CUDA, its proprietary software platform and tools. Morningstar says developers use them to build and train AI models, while the company’s networking products help customers connect GPUs into larger systems for AI training.

The firm sees Nvidia’s position as resting on more than hardware. Its analysis points to CUDA’s role in developer workflows and the cost of switching from the platform as advantages that could help preserve the company’s lead. It also says data-center GPUs and networking have expanded Nvidia’s role in AI infrastructure.

That hardware has roots in graphics and gaming, but the parallel-processing design of GPUs has become useful for accelerating AI workloads. A GPU can process many pieces of data at the same time, while the central processing units used in PCs and servers handle data more serially. The distinction helps explain why a company already known for graphics processors became a central supplier for AI model development and training.

The competitive advantage described in the analysis is cumulative: customers can use Nvidia’s processors, CUDA tools and networking to build systems, while developers have workflows built around the software. Switching to a different chip designer can therefore involve more than comparing hardware. The analysis treats those customer switching costs and the company’s breadth of products as reasons rivals may make progress without quickly replacing Nvidia as the industry leader.

That outlook is not unconditional. Major cloud vendors are seeking in-house solutions to diversify their supply, and AMD is working on data-center GPUs and AI accelerators. The assessment expects those efforts to chip away at Nvidia’s position over time, while tying the company’s longer-term valuation to how quickly AI infrastructure is built out.

Microsoft combines its Azure cloud platform with a large base of business software customers. Morningstar also cites Microsoft’s investment in OpenAI as part of its AI position, and describes Azure as a place for customers to run cloud workloads and use services tied to AI.

The roundup argues that Microsoft can use its existing customer relationships to support cloud adoption. It also suggests Azure could become an orchestration layer for agentic AI, while noting that the company’s growth case includes its broader software and cloud businesses.

Azure’s appeal in the analysis includes a route for customers to experiment with cloud services and move selected workloads while keeping some systems on premises. That hybrid approach can make it easier to shift applications and data within the Microsoft environment. The company can also draw on its installed base of Microsoft products when presenting Azure as an option for customers’ cloud plans.

The AI opportunity is part of a wider set of cloud services rather than the only source of growth in the thesis. Azure is also positioned for business intelligence and Internet of Things services. The analysis describes the platform as a possible orchestration layer for agentic AI, linking that potential to Microsoft’s broader cloud capabilities and relationships with existing customers.

The software business remains relevant to the valuation case as well. Microsoft is known for Windows and Office, and the analysis points to Office 365 upgrades, including higher-priced versions with advanced telephony features. It also describes the company’s move from on-premises software delivery to cloud services as a transition that has already reshaped the business. Gaming is another part of the portfolio, with the company pushing toward recurring revenue and cloud delivery.

The combination of cloud growth, customer ties and established software helps explain why the company is assessed as more than an AI investment alone. The stated outlook anticipates continued revenue growth and improving margins over the next several years, while the fair value comparison remains an estimate rather than a timetable for those results or a promised share-price move.

Morningstar describes Amazon as a leading online retailer and marketplace and says the company dominates cloud services. That establishes why Amazon appears in an AI-stock roundup, but the available analysis does not provide the same level of detail about Amazon’s AI products or investment case as it does for Nvidia and Microsoft.

The company’s broader scale is central to the available description. Its e-commerce business serves consumers and third-party sellers, and its size supports a wide selection of goods at low prices. The analysis also points to continuing gains in e-commerce market share despite Amazon’s already large position, and describes Prime as tying together its retail efforts.

Cloud services provide the direct connection to AI infrastructure in this roundup. Amazon’s position in cloud is presented alongside its e-commerce strength, but the source text available here does not set out particular AI products, spending plans, or a separate AI growth forecast for the company. The $300 fair value estimate and 17% discount are therefore the stated valuation comparison; they should not be read as evidence that Amazon is expected to outperform the other two stocks.

The roundup describes a difficult patch for AI-related shares in October. A semiconductor selloff and concerns about debt-funded spending on AI infrastructure weighed on the sector ahead of earnings season.

At the same time, Morningstar cited strong gains in its Global Next Generation Artificial Intelligence Index: more than 29% year to date and about 45% during the spring. Those index figures show how sharply the AI infrastructure theme had advanced, but do not establish that every AI-linked stock shared the same performance.
